name: Orangey Brown
lede: Orangey Brown is a deep, burnt orange-brown from an online color survey, a hedge between two words that Paterson's dictionary also uses for French yellow.

sections.title: Between two words
sections.body:
The library records Orangey Brown from a 2010 crowd-sourced survey, with a near-duplicate, Orangish Brown, only 0.6 units away [1]. The nearest ISCC-NBS category is deep orange, about 3.2 units away [1]. Its nearest named relatives are [[burnt-orange]], [[saddle-brown]] and [[brown]] [2].

Paterson's *Dictionary of Colour* uses the same words for French yellow, defined as a yellowish or orangey-brown [3]. That makes the phrase older than the survey as plain speech, even if no dictionary lists it as a color [3][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Orangey Brown appears in 286 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 1.2%, as photographed [5]. It peaks in paintings of the 1400s, in 9 of 945 (1.0%), 1.3 times the rate expected from the same museums [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 78% of the 156 paintings where it counts [5]. The painter most devoted to it is Adriaen van Ostade, in 4 of 39 works here [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [5].

questions.q: In Paterson's dictionary, French yellow is described as which kind of color?
In which role does this color most often appear inside a painting?

openers: A burnt orange-brown that paintings use mostly as an accent.
